name: Investing (superficial) layer of deep cervical fascia

bony_attachments.landmark: mastoid process and superior nuchal line
manubrium (splitting to form the suprasternal space)

function: Encircles the entire neck like a collar, splitting to enclose sternocleidomastoid and trapezius; splits again near the sternum to form the suprasternal space (containing the jugular venous arch). The most superficial of the neck's 3 deep fascial layers (deep to platysma and superficial fascia/skin, despite its name).
source: Gray's Anatomy for Students, 4th ed. (Drake, Vogl, Mitchell); Terminologia Anatomica (FICAT 1998); Stecco C, Functional Atlas of the Human Fascial System (2015), Churchill Livingstone

name: Pretracheal layer of deep cervical fascia

bony_attachments.landmark: posterior manubrium (inferior, continuous with the fibrous pericardium)

function: Encloses the infrahyoid ('strap') muscles and the thyroid gland/trachea/esophagus (visceral compartment); contributes to the carotid sheath laterally; its inferior continuation directly into the fibrous pericardium is the anatomical basis for infection or air (pneumomediastinum) tracking from the neck into the mediastinum.
source: Gray's Anatomy for Students, 4th ed. (Drake, Vogl, Mitchell); Terminologia Anatomica (FICAT 1998); Stecco C, Functional Atlas of the Human Fascial System (2015), Churchill Livingstone

name: Prevertebral layer of deep cervical fascia

bony_attachments.landmark: anterior and lateral surfaces of the cervical transverse processes and vertebral bodies

function: Deepest of the 3 layers, forming a tube around the vertebral column and its prevertebral/deep neck flexor muscles; continues laterally over the scalenes as the axillary sheath, carrying the brachial plexus and subclavian vessels into the axilla -- a direct fascial-continuity link between the neck and upper limb.
source: Gray's Anatomy for Students, 4th ed. (Drake, Vogl, Mitchell); Terminologia Anatomica (FICAT 1998); Stecco C, Functional Atlas of the Human Fascial System (2015), Churchill Livingstone

name: Carotid sheath

bony_attachments.landmark: base of skull, around the carotid canal and jugular foramen

function: A condensation classically described as formed by contributions from all 3 cervical fascial layers (investing forming the anterolateral wall, pretracheal the anteromedial wall, prevertebral the posterior wall) -- the standard/majority teaching, though genuinely debated in the anatomical literature, with some authors questioning whether it is truly a discrete structure formed this way versus a looser fascial condensation -- enclosing the common/internal carotid artery, internal jugular vein, and vagus nerve (CN X) together as a single neurovascular bundle running the length of the neck. The vessels these contain are documented in data/vascular/head_neck_arterial.json and head_neck_venous.json.
source: Gray's Anatomy for Students, 4th ed. (Drake, Vogl, Mitchell); Terminologia Anatomica (FICAT 1998); Stecco C, Functional Atlas of the Human Fascial System (2015), Churchill Livingstone

name: Buccopharyngeal fascia
function: Thin fascia covering the outer (buccal) surface of buccinator and continuing posteriorly over the outer surface of the pharyngeal constrictors; the pterygomandibular raphe -- the fibrous line where buccinator and superior pharyngeal constrictor interdigitate -- is the structure this fascia is named for spanning.
source: Gray's Anatomy for Students, 4th ed. (Drake, Vogl, Mitchell); Terminologia Anatomica (FICAT 1998); Stecco C, Functional Atlas of the Human Fascial System (2015), Churchill Livingstone

name: Superficial cervical fascia (platysma layer)
function: Subcutaneous layer enclosing platysma, cutaneous nerves and the superficial veins. Continuous above with the SMAS of the face and below with the superficial fascia of the chest. It is the plane a subplatysmal flap is raised in, and the reason platysma must be reapproximated for a good neck scar.
source: Gray's Anatomy for Students, 4th ed. (Drake, Vogl, Mitchell); Moore KL, Dalley AF, Agur AMR, Clinically Oriented Anatomy, 8th ed.; Terminologia Anatomica (FICAT 1998); Stecco C, Functional Atlas of the Human Fascial System (2015), Churchill Livingstone

name: Alar fascia
function: A thin coronal sheet between the buccopharyngeal and prevertebral layers, running from the skull base to about T2. It is what divides the retropharyngeal space in front from the danger space behind, and so decides how far a deep neck infection can descend.
source: Gray's Anatomy for Students, 4th ed. (Drake, Vogl, Mitchell); Moore KL, Dalley AF, Agur AMR, Clinically Oriented Anatomy, 8th ed.; Terminologia Anatomica (FICAT 1998)

name: Retropharyngeal space
function: Between the buccopharyngeal fascia in front and the alar fascia behind, extending from the skull base to about T2 where the two fuse. Abscess here pushes the pharynx forward and widens the prevertebral soft tissue on a lateral radiograph.
source: Gray's Anatomy for Students, 4th ed. (Drake, Vogl, Mitchell); Moore KL, Dalley AF, Agur AMR, Clinically Oriented Anatomy, 8th ed.; Terminologia Anatomica (FICAT 1998)

name: Danger space (space 4)
function: Between the alar fascia in front and the prevertebral fascia behind. It is named for its extent: unlike the retropharyngeal space it runs uninterrupted from the skull base to the diaphragm, so infection entering it can reach the posterior mediastinum.
source: Gray's Anatomy for Students, 4th ed. (Drake, Vogl, Mitchell); Moore KL, Dalley AF, Agur AMR, Clinically Oriented Anatomy, 8th ed.; Terminologia Anatomica (FICAT 1998)

name: Pretracheal space
function: Enclosed by the pretracheal fascia, continuous inferiorly with the anterior mediastinum -- the descending route for anterior deep neck infection.
source: Gray's Anatomy for Students, 4th ed. (Drake, Vogl, Mitchell); Moore KL, Dalley AF, Agur AMR, Clinically Oriented Anatomy, 8th ed.; Terminologia Anatomica (FICAT 1998)
